subject: prior scales for regression coefficients with vs. without interactions

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: prior scales for regression coefficients with vs. without interactions
parts:
Q1: If you have parameters and interacted parameters, will
you generally have all the parameters being smaller?

Q2: If so, should you then have smaller prior scales for the
lower-level parameters?

Q3: Is there some way to keep the expected sizes of the
basic parameters the same so that the higher-level parameters
just take up the slack?

I'm probably not asking this the right way, but I hope people
know what I mean.

- Bob

messages.author: edd4914c326b6d31
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] prior scales for regression coefficients with vs. without interactions
parts:
On Fri, Oct 04, 2013 at 08:09:52PM -0400, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Q1: If you have parameters and interacted parameters, will
> you generally have all the parameters being smaller?
>
> Q2: If so, should you then have smaller prior scales for the
> lower-level parameters?

The models I was using grouped the coefficients into batches, each of
which had its own scale. Loosely, the batches were based on the
order of the term, e.g., 3 way interactions were in one batch, 2 way
another, and so on.

sigma ~ cauchy(0, 5) //sigma a vector
beta[i] ~ normal(0, sigma[sdclass[i]])
where sdclass gives the group that beta[i] is in.

Also, parameterization used R's contr.sum, so that the sum of effects
across levels is 0. I thought that might help with the scaling if the
higher order interactions were smaller.

>
> Q3: Is there some way to keep the expected sizes of the
> basic parameters the same so that the higher-level parameters
> just take up the slack?
Does the contr.sum coding address that?

>
> I'm probably not asking this the right way, but I hope people
> know what I mean.

I'm not sure I follow, in particular about why it matters if the
scales are smaller or larger.

I think you are comparing estimates for A in 2 models:
I) y ~ A + B (R notation for y as a function of 2 main effects)
II) y ~ A + B + A:B (A:B is the interaction).

and then you are asking about the magnitude of the effects estimated
for the A term in I and II.

Ross
